docs.title: Who I am and what I offer
docs.content: I am Maya Ortiz, a residential agent in Austin, Texas. I work with first-time buyers who are nervous about making offers, and with sellers who want a clean, quick sale. I offer a free 20 minute buyer plan call. I always explain closing costs up front, before anyone tours a home.

docs.title: Recent results
docs.content: Last quarter I closed 9 homes. Six were first-time buyers. Two of them won against several offers without waiving inspections, by writing a short personal letter and offering a flexible closing date. Average time from first call to accepted offer for buyers was about five weeks.

docs.title: Post: your offer is a story
docs.content: Your offer is not just a number. It is a story the seller can picture. A short letter, clean terms and a flexible closing date beat a bigger number surprisingly often. Say it plainly. Call me before you tour a fifth house.

docs.title: What I build
docs.content: I maintain Pilewise, an open source TypeScript toolkit for background jobs that runs on Postgres. No Redis. It handles retries, scheduling and a small dashboard with a few lines of config. It is MIT licensed and used by small SaaS teams.

docs.title: Proof
docs.content: I moved an app running about 40 thousand jobs a day from a cron script plus Redis to Pilewise in one afternoon. I deleted around 400 lines of code and the retry bugs went away. Median job pickup time stayed under 50 milliseconds on a small instance.

docs.title: Post: queue bugs are retry bugs
docs.content: Most queue bugs are retry bugs. Make every job idempotent, give it a unique key, and let the database be the lock. Then you stop writing clever code. Show the code, run it, ship it.

docs.title: What I do
docs.content: I run positioning and launch work for B2B software teams. My playbook is simple: one customer problem, one sentence of positioning, one proof point, and one message test every week.

docs.title: Proof
docs.content: A headline test on a pricing page lifted trial starts by about a third over four weeks at a 60 person software company. A launch rebuilt around the customer's problem instead of the feature list doubled demo requests from the launch email.

docs.title: Post: lead with the problem
docs.content: Your homepage lists features. Your buyer is thinking about a problem. Lead with the problem in their words, then show the feature as the answer. Test one line a week. Keep the winner.

docs.title: Context
docs.content: I am the CEO of a 120 person B2B software company that sells to finance teams. I post once a week about decisions, hiring and what I got wrong. No hype, no slogans.

docs.title: Recent decisions
docs.content: We paused two product lines to focus on one. We hired a head of customer success before a head of sales. Revenue grew faster once we stopped chasing every request. Churn fell after I joined weekly customer calls.

docs.title: Post: what I got wrong
docs.content: I said yes to too many customers this year. Every yes felt like growth. Together they slowed us down. This quarter I said no more than I said yes, and the team shipped faster. Focus is a decision you repeat.

docs.title: Context
docs.content: I am a solo founder building a scheduling tool for independent clinics, in public. I have 14 paying clinics and about 6 thousand dollars in monthly revenue, with no ads. I share the real numbers every month.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.content: I charged from day one and learned more in a week than in three months of free beta. I nearly quit in the spring after losing two clinics in one week, then fixed onboarding and both came back. The biggest unlock was calling every customer who churned.

docs.title: Post: call the people who left
docs.content: Call every customer who leaves. Not a survey, a call. In five minutes you learn what a hundred emails will not tell you. I fixed onboarding because of two calls. Both customers came back.
